newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi sanctions group sends signal to regime.
newsitem.headline: Burundi sanctions group sends signal to regime.

text.p: The African committee enforcing sanctions against Burundi sent a small olive branch to military leader Pierre Buyoya on Thursday.

The committee recommended that Buyoya "be invited to be available" for the next regional summit to discuss policy on Burundi where ethnic war has killed at least 150,000 majority Hutus and minority Tutsis since 1993.
But while the government welcomed the statement as positive, it said sanctions on the landlocked country should be lifted immediately.
"We have received the declaration...and we consider that it is a good thing...to (finally) be able to explain the situation to our neighbours," said information minister Pierre-Claver Ndayicariye.
"There are problems with vaccines, with medicine, the agricultural chemicals, people who have died...."
"It is never too late to make peace, but while people hesitate about lifting sanctions, the embargo claims innocent victims," he said in an interview.
He was unable to say if Buyoya would attend the meeting, to which the committee said "other leaders of parties to the conflict...also be invited to be available".
Previously, leaders and officials from pro-sanctions countries ignored or rejected Buyoya's pleas to be given a top-level hearing on why the army took power on July 25.
No date for the next summit has been set.
The sanctions committee, in its communique after meeting in the Rwandan capital on Wednesday, said the economic and transport embargo imposed on landlocked Burundi on July 31 had been effective.
Fuel and other key imports are in short supply and most of Burundi's tea and coffee exports are blocked.
The committee said it noted "the positive steps taken by the Buyoya regime" in lifting a ban on political parties and restoring parliament.
But it said Buyoya had not fully met the most important condition set by regional leaders, namely immediate and unconditional talks with all groups.
The committee's recommendations have to be approved by ministers of the same countries and the committee recommended they meet on October 10 at an unspecified location.
Ndayicariye said the government had offered to hold talks with rebels, but leaders of the revolt had rejected any negotiations with Buyoya's regime.
Buyoya and the Tutsi-dominated army have not held talks with the main Hutu rebels led by Leonard Nyangoma.
The sanctions committee is made up of Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Zaire and Zambia as well as the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).
Zaire and current OAU chairman Cameroon did not send representatives to the Kigali meeting, the committee said.
